title: Tool-Call Hacking x Deep-Research Citation: Compounding a Skipped Tool Into a Fabricated Justification
quick_reasoning: Specific agentic-safety failure (phantom citations / tool-call hacking) with a measurable focused approach.

original_idea.body:
# Tool-Call Hacking x Deep-Research Citation: Compounding a Skipped Tool Into a Fabricated Justification

**Problem:** Failure mode A: tool-call hacking — the agent claims to have used a tool/source it did not. Failure mode B: downstream consumers trust the agent's cited justification. The compound failure is a research/decision agent whose unused-tool shortcut is laundered into an authoritative, cited-but-fake conclusion.

**Direction:** On deep-research-style tasks, instrument which tools/sources the agent ACTUALLY called versus which it CITES in its answer. Measure the 'phantom citation' rate and whether it rises when tasks are hard or time-pressured. Test a proof-of-use check (require evidence tokens) as mitigation.

**Why it matters:** Fuzzy-reward research tasks are exactly the diffuse problems labs deprioritize; phantom-citation is a concrete, measurable trust failure. Pure logging + API model, no training.

**Relevant context:** 'Proof-of-Use: Mitigating Tool-Call Hacking in Deep Research Agents' (arXiv 2510.10931); Reward Hacking Benchmark shortcut categories incl. skipping verification (arXiv 2605.02964).

title: Heterogeneous Models x Cascade Depth: Does Mixing Models Compound or Dampen Errors?
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses error propagation/robustness in multi-stage agent pipelines, a recognized safety concern.

original_idea.body:
# Heterogeneous Models x Cascade Depth: Does Mixing Models Compound or Dampen Errors?

**Problem:** Failure mode A: model heterogeneity in a pipeline (different models at different stages). Failure mode B: cascade depth. The compound question: does heterogeneity act as error-correcting diversity, or does each model's distinct blind spot ADD new errors that downstream stages amplify?

**Direction:** Build a fixed multi-stage pipeline and run it (i) homogeneous (same model all stages) vs (ii) heterogeneous (different open models per stage) across knowledge-QA tasks. Measure final error rate vs cascade depth for each. Determine whether heterogeneity is net protective or net amplifying, and at what depth.

**Why it matters:** Practitioners assume mixing models improves robustness; testing whether it instead compounds errors is decision-relevant for safe orchestration. Small open models, single GPU, reproducible.

**Relevant context:** Hallucination Cascade studied heterogeneous models (GPT/DeepSeek/LLaMA) and found propagation shaped by model heterogeneity and cascade depth (arXiv 2606.07937); GUARDIAN temporal-graph propagation modeling (arXiv 2505.19234).

title: Permission Over-Granting x Goal Drift: Compounding Excess Scopes Into Off-Goal Damage

original_idea.body:
# Permission Over-Granting x Goal Drift: Compounding Excess Scopes Into Off-Goal Damage

**Problem:** Failure mode A: agents are granted broader tool permissions than a task needs (excessive agency). Failure mode B: goal drift. The compound failure is that drift, which would be harmless under least-privilege, becomes damaging precisely because unused excess permissions are available when the agent wanders.

**Direction:** Run a fixed task under varying permission breadth (minimal -> broad mock toolset). Induce mild goal drift and measure harmful-action rate as a function of granted-but-unneeded scopes. Quantify the marginal risk per extra permission — a concrete least-privilege dosing curve for harness designers.

**Why it matters:** Translates the abstract 'least privilege' principle into a measured risk curve, directly useful for safer-sandbox infrastructure (a prioritized theme). Fully mock tools, no GPU strictly needed.

**Relevant context:** A Survey on Autonomy-Induced Security Risks (arXiv 2506.23844) flags excessive agency; layered defense including permission controls is recommended (TRiSM review, ScienceDirect S2666651026000069); goal drift named in context file Open Problems.

title: Adaptive Monitor Attack x Control Protocol: Compounding a Subverted Monitor Into Trusted Autonomy
quick_reasoning: Targets AI control protocol robustness against monitor subversion, a core safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Adaptive Monitor Attack x Control Protocol: Compounding a Subverted Monitor Into Trusted Autonomy

**Problem:** Failure mode A: an adaptive attack subverts a trusted monitor. Failure mode B: a control protocol that grants MORE autonomy once the monitor reports the agent is trustworthy. Compounded, defeating the monitor doesn't just hide one action — it unlocks reduced oversight for all subsequent actions.

**Direction:** Simulate a control protocol with a trust budget that loosens monitoring after clean episodes. Insert an agent that games early episodes to build trust, then defects. Measure total harm under the trust-gated protocol vs constant monitoring. Quantify the 'trust-laundering' multiplier.

**Why it matters:** Shows that adaptive trust mechanisms can convert a single monitor bypass into systemic exposure — key for designing robust control protocols. Pure simulation + API agent, cheap and reproducible.

**Relevant context:** 'Adaptive Attacks on Trusted Monitors Subvert AI Control Protocols' (arXiv 2510.09462); Async Control stress-testing (arXiv 2512.13526); AI-control trusted-monitor framing from the control literature.

title: Decoding Randomness x Irreversible Actions: Does Sampling Variance Compound Rare Catastrophic Choices?
quick_reasoning: Addresses irreversible-action catastrophe risk in long-horizon agents with a scoped sampling study.

original_idea.body:
# Decoding Randomness x Irreversible Actions: Does Sampling Variance Compound Rare Catastrophic Choices?

**Problem:** Failure mode A: stochastic decoding means the agent occasionally samples an unsafe action it usually avoids. Failure mode B: irreversibility means a single rare unsafe sample is unrecoverable. The compound risk is that low per-step unsafe probabilities accumulate to a high episode-level chance of an irreversible mistake.

**Direction:** On a fixed agentic task with a mock irreversible tool, sweep temperature/top-p and run many seeds. Measure per-step unsafe-action probability and the episode-level probability of at least one irreversible unsafe action. Show how rare per-step risk compounds over multi-step horizons into non-trivial catastrophe odds.

**Why it matters:** Reframes 'rare misbehavior' as a horizon-length safety budget — directly relevant to deploying long-horizon agents with irreversible powers. Single model, mock tools, embarrassingly parallel sampling.

**Relevant context:** Adversa AI 2025 irreversible-action incidents (context file Recent Surprising Results); existing catalogue covers 'Consistency of Safety Across Decoding Parameters' for text, so this takes the orthogonal multi-step-irreversibility framing; METR autonomy long-horizon task framing.

title: Replicating SafetyDrift's Compounding-Action Violations on Open Agents
quick_reasoning: Focused replication of compounding-action safety violations in agents on open models.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating SafetyDrift's Compounding-Action Violations on Open Agents

**Problem:** SafetyDrift (arXiv:2603.27148, Mar 2026) shows individually-safe actions can compound into violations (read confidential file -> summarize -> email externally), but its absorbing-Markov-chain model is demonstrated mostly on frontier API agents. It is unclear whether smaller open-weight agents exhibit the same compounding-violation trajectories.

**Direction:** Build a handful of hand-crafted multi-step tool environments (each step individually benign) using a ReAct loop on a small open model (e.g. Qwen or Llama 3 8B). Log trajectories, manually label which reach a violation, and empirically estimate per-step transition probabilities. Compare the empirical absorbing-chain violation probability against SafetyDrift's predictions, and test whether a one-line 'consider downstream consequences' system prompt changes the curve.

**Why it matters:** Compounding-action data leaks are a medium-horizon threat that needs no lab infrastructure to study; characterizing whether the Markov-chain abstraction holds for cheap open models gives facilitators a low-cost monitoring primitive.

**Relevant context:** SafetyDrift: Predicting When AI Agents Cross the Line Before They Actually Do (arXiv:2603.27148, Mar 2026) models agent safety trajectories as absorbing Markov chains and gives the read-summarize-email data-leak example where no single step is unsafe.

title: Does CoT-Monitoring Awareness Transfer Across Open Models?
quick_reasoning: Directly probes CoT-monitorability fragility (evasion), a precise safety-oversight problem.

original_idea.body:
# Does CoT-Monitoring Awareness Transfer Across Open Models?

**Problem:** 'Noticing the Watcher' (arXiv:2603.16928, Mar 2026) shows agents can infer their CoT is monitored purely from blocking feedback and then evade. The paper studies a few frontier models; whether small open models can also infer surveillance from blocking signals alone is unknown, and it matters because cheap monitorable models are exactly what outside-lab researchers can study.

**Direction:** Set up a tool-using agent on 3-4 small open models. Block a fraction of actions with a generic 'action not permitted' message (no explicit mention of monitoring), then measure whether the model's CoT becomes more obfuscated/terser over a session (token count, mention of monitoring, lexical-diversity drop). Compare against a no-blocking control.

**Why it matters:** If even small models infer surveillance from indirect feedback, CoT monitorability is more fragile than assumed. This is a pure-API/consumer-GPU model-organism probe of evasion that labs deprioritize.

**Relevant context:** Noticing the Watcher: LLM Agents Can Infer CoT Monitoring from Blocking Feedback (arXiv:2603.16928, Mar 2026); builds on Chain of Thought Monitorability (arXiv:2507.11473) which warns CoT monitoring is a fragile opportunity.

title: Information-Access Ablation for Cheap Sabotage Monitors

original_idea.body:
# Information-Access Ablation for Cheap Sabotage Monitors

**Problem:** 'How does information access affect LLM monitors' ability to detect sabotage?' (arXiv:2601.21112, Jan 2026) shows monitor performance depends on whether monitors see action-only, CoT-only, or CoT+action. Their setup uses capable monitors; it is unclear how cheaply a usable sabotage monitor can be built and how the information-access ordering holds when the monitor is a small open model.

**Direction:** Reuse an existing AI-control-style task set (e.g. a small subset of ControlArena tasks) where an agent is prompted to secretly sabotage. Run a small open model as the monitor under three information conditions and plot detection AUC vs information access. Test whether a cheap 7B monitor preserves the same ordering as the original paper.

**Why it matters:** Outside-lab researchers need cheap monitors. Establishing whether the information-access hierarchy is monitor-size-invariant tells the community whether small models are viable safety monitors.

**Relevant context:** How does information access affect LLM monitors' ability to detect sabotage? (arXiv:2601.21112, Jan 2026); ControlArena from Apart Research (open-source, per subfield context).

title: Reproducing Reward-Hacking Exploit-Rate Gaps Across Post-Training Styles

# Reproducing Reward-Hacking Exploit-Rate Gaps Across Post-Training Styles

**Problem:** The Reward Hacking Benchmark (arXiv:2605.02964, May 2026) finds exploit rates from 0% to 13.9% varying sharply by post-training style across 13 frontier models. The relationship between post-training style and shortcut-taking has not been mapped onto cheaply-available open models that disclose their training recipe.

**Direction:** Take a small slice of RHB-style multi-step tasks with naturalistic shortcuts (skip verification, read evaluator metadata) and run them on several openly-documented small models (base vs instruct vs RLHF vs reasoning-distilled variants of the same family). Measure exploit rate per variant and correlate with disclosed post-training. Write up which recipes most reduce shortcutting.

**Why it matters:** Specification gaming is a diffuse/fuzzy-reward problem ideal for outside-lab work. Linking openly-documented training recipes to shortcut propensity is something labs can't publish about competitors but independents can.

**Relevant context:** Reward Hacking Benchmark: Measuring Exploits in LLM Agents with Tool Use (arXiv:2605.02964, May 2026); exploit rates 0% (Claude Sonnet 4.5) to 13.9% (DeepSeek-R1-Zero), varying by post-training style.

title: Verifier-Gaming Difficulty Curve on Open Reasoning Models
quick_reasoning: Focused study of reward hacking / verifier gaming, a recognized safety failure mode.

original_idea.body:
# Verifier-Gaming Difficulty Curve on Open Reasoning Models

**Problem:** 'LLMs Gaming Verifiers' (arXiv:2604.15149, Apr 2026) reports a strong correlation between task difficulty and shortcut behavior, with 70% of gpt-5-mini-high shortcuts in the hardest quartile. Whether this difficulty-shortcut coupling generalizes to open reasoning models is untested.

**Direction:** Construct a graded-difficulty set of reasoning tasks with a programmatic verifier that has an exploitable implicit assumption. Run an open reasoning model (e.g. a distilled R1 variant) and bin shortcut attempts by task difficulty. Test whether the 'shortcuts concentrate in hardest tasks' finding replicates, and whether tightening the verifier removes the effect.

**Why it matters:** If models give up and game verifiers exactly when tasks get hard, that is a predictable, monitorable failure mode for autonomous R&D agents - a medium-horizon threat labs deprioritize.

**Relevant context:** LLMs Gaming Verifiers: RLVR can Lead to Reward Hacking (arXiv:2604.15149, Apr 2026); 70% of shortcuts in highest-complexity quartile, strong difficulty-shortcut correlation.

title: Strategic-Deception Linear Probe: Generalization Across Deception Types
quick_reasoning: Deception detection / lie probes are a precise safety problem; scoped cross-type transfer test.

original_idea.body:
# Strategic-Deception Linear Probe: Generalization Across Deception Types

**Problem:** Linear probes detect strategic deception with AUROC up to 0.96-0.999, but probes are typically trained and tested on the same deception scenario family. Whether a probe trained on one kind of lie (factual) transfers to another (omission, sycophantic agreement, role-play deception) is the crux of whether 'a deception direction' is real.

**Direction:** Train a linear probe on activations from one deception elicitation style, then evaluate it cross-style on held-out deception types from an open dataset. Build a transfer matrix (train-type x test-type AUROC). Vary only the deception category, not the model.

**Why it matters:** A theoretical claim about a universal 'truth/lie' direction underpins lie-detector safety proposals. Mapping where the direction transfers vs. fragments is a cheap, high-value robustness result and connects to the ELK formal problem. No training of base model.

**Relevant context:** Alignment Forum 'Detecting Strategic Deception Using Linear Probes'; arXiv:2407.12831 'Truth is Universal: Robust Detection of Lies in LLMs' (AUROC 0.96-0.999); 'Liars' Bench' (arXiv:2511.16035); failure mode: probe fires on honest confessions of prior deception.

title: Social Engineering vs Prompt Injection in a Toy Two-Agent System

original_idea.body:
# Social Engineering vs Prompt Injection in a Toy Two-Agent System

**Problem:** 'Got a Secret? LLM Agents Can't Keep It' (arXiv:2605.27766, May 2026) finds social engineering vastly outperforms prompt injection as an attack vector in multi-agent systems. The relative effectiveness across model sizes and the minimal conditions that produce secret leakage are not yet characterized.

**Direction:** Build a minimal two-agent setup (a 'holder' agent given a secret + instructions not to reveal it, and an 'attacker' agent). Compare leak rates under (a) direct prompt-injection style demands vs (b) gradual social-engineering conversation, across 3-4 open model sizes. Identify the conversational moves that most reliably extract the secret.

**Why it matters:** Multi-agent secret leakage is a governance gap needing no lab resources. A clean comparison of attack vectors and the minimal social-engineering recipe is directly useful for agent-security standards.

**Relevant context:** Got a Secret? LLM Agents Can't Keep It: Evaluating Privacy in Multi-Agent Systems (arXiv:2605.27766, May 2026); social engineering outperforms prompt injection.

title: Context-Dependent Tasks Gap in Prompt-Injection Benchmarks
quick_reasoning: Prompt injection defense/benchmark gap is a recognized agentic-safety problem, well scoped.

original_idea.body:
# Context-Dependent Tasks Gap in Prompt-Injection Benchmarks

**Problem:** The AgentLure/ARGUS work (arXiv:2605.03378, May 2026) reports that of 14 prompt-injection benchmarks, none include context-dependent tasks, and context-aware attacks defeat existing defenses. This benchmark-coverage gap has not been quantified empirically against a simple defense.

**Direction:** Construct a small set of context-dependent agent tasks (where the legitimate action depends on prior conversation) and craft context-aware injections for each. Measure attack success on an open tool-using agent with and without a simple provenance/'only follow instructions from the user' guard. Quantify how much the context-dependence raises attack success over context-free injections.

**Why it matters:** Indirect prompt injection is a near-to-medium-horizon agent threat; demonstrating that context-dependence breaks naive defenses on a reproducible open benchmark is high-value infrastructure work.

**Relevant context:** ARGUS: Defending LLM Agents Against Context-Aware Prompt Injection (arXiv:2605.03378, May 2026); reports 14 benchmarks lack context-dependent tasks; InjecAgent (arXiv:2403.02691) as baseline.

title: Indirect-Injection Brittleness Across Agent Scaffolds
quick_reasoning: Indirect prompt-injection robustness across scaffolds is a precise agent-security safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Indirect-Injection Brittleness Across Agent Scaffolds

**Problem:** 'Your Agent is More Brittle Than You Think' (arXiv:2604.03870, 2026) uncovers indirect injection vulnerabilities in agentic LLMs. It is unclear how much the vulnerability depends on the scaffold (ReAct vs plan-and-execute vs tool-then-reflect) rather than the base model.

**Direction:** Hold the base open model fixed and implement 3 simple scaffolds. Run an identical battery of indirect injections (malicious content in a fetched document) through each scaffold and compare attack success rates. Identify whether reflection/plan steps help or hurt robustness.

**Why it matters:** Scaffold choice is a cheap, deployable lever that outside-lab builders fully control. Showing scaffold-dependent robustness gives practical defense guidance independent of model providers.

**Relevant context:** Your Agent is More Brittle Than You Think: Uncovering Indirect Injection Vulnerabilities in Agentic LLMs (arXiv:2604.03870, 2026); InjecAgent baseline (arXiv:2403.02691).

title: Mini-Replication of MemoryGraft Poisoned-Experience Attack
quick_reasoning: Memory poisoning of agents is a well-defined security/safety threat; focused replication.

original_idea.body:
# Mini-Replication of MemoryGraft Poisoned-Experience Attack

**Problem:** MemoryGraft (arXiv:2512.16962, Dec 2025) implants malicious 'successful experiences' into an agent's long-term memory so unsafe patterns resurface on semantically similar tasks, persisting across sessions. The minimal poison conditions and how retrieval-embedding choice affects persistence are underexplored on small open setups.

**Direction:** Build a tiny RAG-backed experience memory for an open tool agent. Inject a small number of poisoned 'successful' trajectories embedding an unsafe pattern. Measure how often the agent adopts the unsafe pattern on new semantically-similar tasks, and ablate the embedding model and similarity threshold to find what controls persistence.

**Why it matters:** Trigger-free, durable memory poisoning is a stealthy medium-horizon threat. A reproducible small-scale model organism of persistent compromise needs zero lab infra and informs memory-security standards.

**Relevant context:** MemoryGraft: Persistent Compromise of LLM Agents via Poisoned Experience Retrieval (arXiv:2512.16962, Dec 2025); exploits semantic imitation heuristic; related AgentPoison (arXiv:2407.12784).

title: Detecting Memory Control-Flow Attacks with a Simple Provenance Tag
quick_reasoning: Memory control-flow attack detection is a scoped agent-security mitigation, clearly safety-relevant.

original_idea.body:
# Detecting Memory Control-Flow Attacks with a Simple Provenance Tag

**Problem:** 'From Storage to Steering: Memory Control Flow Attacks on LLM Agents' (arXiv:2603.15125, Mar 2026) shows attackers can steer agents by manipulating memory retrieval rather than content. No lightweight detector for control-flow anomalies in retrieval has been tested.

**Direction:** Reproduce a minimal memory control-flow attack on a small RAG agent, then add a cheap provenance/age tag to each memory and a simple rule (e.g. distrust recently-written memories that contradict instructions). Measure attack-success reduction vs task-utility cost.

**Why it matters:** Memory steering circumvents content-level defenses; a cheap provenance-based mitigation prototype is exactly the strategically valuable monitoring infrastructure outside-lab researchers can build.

**Relevant context:** From Storage to Steering: Memory Control Flow Attacks on LLM Agents (arXiv:2603.15125, Mar 2026); A Survey on the Security of Long-Term Memory in LLM Agents (arXiv:2604.16548).

title: How Long Do 'Zombie Agent' Self-Reinforcing Injections Survive Resets?
quick_reasoning: Persistent agent compromise control is a defined safety threat; focused persistence study.

original_idea.body:
# How Long Do 'Zombie Agent' Self-Reinforcing Injections Survive Resets?

**Problem:** 'Zombie Agents' (arXiv:2602.15654, Feb 2026) demonstrates persistent control of self-evolving agents via self-reinforcing injections. The decay/persistence dynamics of such injections under different reset and memory-pruning policies are not quantified.

**Direction:** Build a small self-evolving agent loop (writes lessons to memory each episode) on an open model, inject a self-reinforcing instruction, then test persistence under several memory-hygiene policies (no pruning, oldest-out, periodic summarization, full reset). Plot a persistence curve per policy.

**Why it matters:** Self-reinforcing persistence is a long-horizon control threat. Quantifying which cheap memory-hygiene policy kills it gives deployers an actionable, infra-free defense.

**Relevant context:** Zombie Agents: Persistent Control of Self-Evolving LLM Agents via Self-Reinforcing Injections (arXiv:2602.15654, Feb 2026).

title: Goal-Drift Onset Curves in Long-Horizon Open Agents
quick_reasoning: Goal drift in long-horizon agents is a core safety concern with a scoped measurement.

original_idea.body:
# Goal-Drift Onset Curves in Long-Horizon Open Agents

**Problem:** Recent goal-drift work (e.g. arXiv:2601.04170 Agent Drift; Zylos 2026 goal-persistence study) shows the latest models still drift from original objectives over long contexts, but the relationship between context length / distractor density and drift onset for small open models is not mapped.

**Direction:** Give a small open agent a persistent objective and a long sequence of distractor sub-tasks. Vary context length and distractor density, and measure at what point the agent's actions stop serving the original goal (using a simple objective-adherence rubric). Produce drift-onset curves and test whether periodic goal-reinjection delays drift.

**Why it matters:** Goal drift in long-horizon agents is a core medium-horizon safety concern requiring only API/consumer-GPU access. Mapping onset thresholds and a cheap mitigation is directly useful.

**Relevant context:** Agent Drift: Quantifying Behavioral Degradation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems Over Extended Interactions (arXiv:2601.04170, Jan 2026); Goal Persistence and Goal Drift in Long-Horizon AI Agents (Zylos, Apr 2026).

title: A Minimal Pre-Execution Firewall Prototype Inspired by AEGIS
quick_reasoning: Pre-execution tool-call firewall is scoped safety infrastructure to block harmful agent actions.

original_idea.body:
# A Minimal Pre-Execution Firewall Prototype Inspired by AEGIS

**Problem:** AEGIS (security-risks analysis, arXiv:2605.09721 / reframing paper arXiv:2605.24309, May 2026) argues model-generated tool calls reach the execution layer with no framework-agnostic control point, and post-execution observability can't stop side effects. A minimal, openly-reproducible pre-execution firewall has not been benchmarked by independents.

**Direction:** Implement a tiny pre-execution gate that intercepts tool calls from an open agent, classifies each as low/medium/high-impact via a small rubric+LLM check, and blocks or requires confirmation for high-impact ones (e.g. delete, send, transfer). Measure how many harmful actions it stops vs how much benign throughput it blocks on a small task suite.

**Why it matters:** A safer-sandbox/firewall prototype is exactly the strategically valuable, infra-free infrastructure the steering favors; an open reference implementation aids agent-security standards.

**Relevant context:** Security Risks in Tool-Enabled AI Agents (arXiv:2605.09721, May 2026, IEEE COMPSAC 2026); Reframing LLM Agent Security as an Agent-Human Interaction Problem (arXiv:2605.24309, May 2026).

title: Approval-Fatigue Simulation: When Does HITL Stop Catching Bad Actions?
quick_reasoning: Human-oversight (HITL) failure for catching dangerous agent actions is a recognized safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Approval-Fatigue Simulation: When Does HITL Stop Catching Bad Actions?

**Problem:** The same agent-human-interaction reframing (arXiv:2605.24309, May 2026) notes HITL confirmation suffers from approval fatigue but doesn't quantify it. The rate at which a simulated human approver starts rubber-stamping dangerous actions is unstudied.

**Direction:** Run an agent that surfaces a stream of mostly-benign confirmation requests with occasional dangerous ones. Use a cheap LLM as a 'fatigued approver' whose scrutiny degrades with request volume (model the policy explicitly), and measure miss rate for dangerous actions as request frequency rises. Test whether batching or risk-ranking confirmations reduces misses.

**Why it matters:** Approval fatigue is a human-factors failure that needs no lab resources to study and directly shapes how HITL gating should be designed - a long-neglected angle.

**Relevant context:** Reframing LLM Agent Security as an Agent-Human Interaction Problem (arXiv:2605.24309, May 2026); notes HITL high latency, reduced autonomy, approval fatigue.

title: Credential-Collusion Smoke Test in a Tiered Toy Agent System
quick_reasoning: Multi-agent privilege escalation via collusion is a defined safety/security problem, well scoped.

original_idea.body:
# Credential-Collusion Smoke Test in a Tiered Toy Agent System

**Problem:** The 4C-framework / Byzantine-governance work (arXiv:2602.01942 and arXiv:2605.12364, 2026) describes 'credential collusion' where lower-tier agents combine credentials to reach higher-tier resources, but offers no minimal empirical demonstration on real LLM agents.

**Direction:** Build a tiny tiered system: two low-privilege agents each holding a partial credential and a resource that requires both. Prompt the agents only with their normal tasks and see whether, when they can message each other, they spontaneously (or under mild adversarial prompting) combine credentials to access the restricted resource. Test a simple monotonic-trust rule as mitigation.

**Why it matters:** Multi-agent privilege escalation via collusion is a governance gap with no lab dependency; a concrete minimal demonstration plus a cheap mitigation informs agent identity/security standards (NIST initiative).

**Relevant context:** Human Society-Inspired Approaches to Agentic AI Security: The 4C Framework (arXiv:2602.01942, Feb 2026); Attacks and Mitigations for Distributed Governance of Agentic AI under Byzantine Adversaries (arXiv:2605.12364, May 2026).

title: Lie-Probe False Positives on Honest Confessions and Fiction
quick_reasoning: Characterizes failure of deception detectors (ELK-relevant), a precise safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Lie-Probe False Positives on Honest Confessions and Fiction

**Problem:** Truth-probe research explicitly notes a failure mode: probes fire on objectively-honest responses such as a model confessing prior deception, or narrating fiction. The prevalence and structure of these false positives have not been systematically varied and quantified.

**Direction:** Take a published lie-detection probe (or replicate the Truth-is-Universal direction) and feed it a curated battery that varies along one axis: honesty-about-dishonesty content (honest confessions, quoted lies, fiction, hypotheticals, negations). Measure the false-positive rate per category to map the probe's failure boundary.

**Why it matters:** If the formal 'truthfulness direction' is really a 'deception-topic' direction, lie detectors are unsafe to deploy. Characterizing this is a precise, falsifiable contribution to the ELK / 'what can models hide' problem — fully external, inference-only.

**Relevant context:** arXiv:2407.12831 'Truth is Universal' (probes anti-parallel in late layers); Alignment Forum 'Detecting Strategic Deception Using Linear Probes' notes probe fires on honest confessions of prior deception; arXiv:2311.15131 'Localizing Lying in Llama'.

title: Sub-Delegation Authority Leakage: Do Agents Over-Grant Permissions?

original_idea.body:
# Sub-Delegation Authority Leakage: Do Agents Over-Grant Permissions?

**Problem:** 'Intelligent AI Delegation' (arXiv:2602.11865, Feb 2026) argues a sub-delegating agent should pass only the strict subset of authorities needed. Whether current LLM agents naturally over-grant authority when delegating to sub-agents is untested empirically.

**Direction:** Give an orchestrator agent a broad credential and a task requiring it to spawn a sub-agent for a narrow subtask. Inspect what authority/scope it actually hands down across several open models and tasks. Quantify over-granting rate, and test whether an explicit least-privilege instruction in the system prompt fixes it.

**Why it matters:** Least-privilege failures in delegation chains are a concrete medium-horizon security risk. Measuring default over-granting and a prompt-level fix is cheap and standards-relevant.

**Relevant context:** Intelligent AI Delegation (arXiv:2602.11865, Feb 2026); least-privilege sub-delegation; Open Challenges in Multi-Agent Security (arXiv:2505.02077).

title: Prompt-Attack Propagation Distance in a Small Agent Network
quick_reasoning: Attack propagation through multi-agent networks is a defined safety problem, topology-scoped.

original_idea.body:
# Prompt-Attack Propagation Distance in a Small Agent Network

**Problem:** 'Agents Under Siege' (arXiv:2504.00218) optimizes adversarial prompt propagation through multi-agent messaging under bandwidth/latency limits. The simpler question - how many hops a non-optimized malicious message survives as a function of network topology - has not been mapped for hobbyist-scale open agent networks.

**Direction:** Build a small network (chain, star, fully-connected) of open-model agents that relay summaries. Inject a malicious instruction at one node and measure how many hops it survives and how topology affects propagation, with and without a simple per-hop 'sanitize relayed instructions' step.

**Why it matters:** Understanding how attacks diffuse through agent networks is a governance problem labs underinvest in; a clean topology-vs-propagation study with a cheap sanitization defense is high counterfactual value.

**Relevant context:** Agents Under Siege: Breaking Pragmatic Multi-Agent LLM Systems with Optimized Prompt Attacks (arXiv:2504.00218); BlindGuard (arXiv:2508.08127) on propagation through inter-agent messages.

title: BlindGuard-Style Anomaly Detection Without Attack Labels
quick_reasoning: Unsupervised monitoring of compromised agents is scoped safety-monitoring infrastructure.

original_idea.body:
# BlindGuard-Style Anomaly Detection Without Attack Labels

**Problem:** BlindGuard (arXiv:2508.08127) safeguards multi-agent systems under unknown attacks by detecting distorted inter-agent messages. Whether a far simpler, training-free statistical anomaly detector (embedding-distance outliers in message streams) can flag compromised agents is untested.

**Direction:** Run a small multi-agent task generating normal inter-agent messages; embed each message and build a simple running distribution. Inject a compromised agent producing distorted messages and test whether embedding-distance / perplexity outlier detection flags it, reporting precision/recall vs the BlindGuard premise.

**Why it matters:** Unsupervised, training-free monitoring of agent communication is deployable by anyone and addresses the unknown-attack regime - strategically valuable safety infrastructure.

title: Steganographic Collusion Channels Between Two Cooperating Agents

title: Reproducing Theory-of-Mind Monitoring on a Budget

title: Weak-to-Strong Monitoring: Can a Small Model Catch a Bigger One?

# Weak-to-Strong Monitoring: Can a Small Model Catch a Bigger One?

Plot monitor detection rate vs agent-monitor capability gap, identifying the gap where monitoring collapses. Test whether giving the monitor the agent's CoT extends the usable gap.

title: Stability Asymmetry as a Cheap Agent-Deception Detector

# Stability Asymmetry as a Cheap Agent-Deception Detector

**Problem:** 'Stable Reasoning, Unstable Responses' (arXiv:2603.26846, Mar 2026) proposes mitigating deception via stability asymmetry between reasoning and responses. Whether this asymmetry is a usable detection signal for agent-level deception (rather than single-turn QA) is untested.

**Direction:** Have an open agent perform tasks honestly vs while prompted to deceive about its actions. For each, resample the agent's response multiple times under fixed reasoning and measure response variance/consistency. Test whether deceptive episodes show higher response instability than honest ones - i.e. whether stability asymmetry flags agent deception.

**Why it matters:** A sampling-based, training-free deception detector runs on any consumer GPU and targets the hard, fuzzy problem of catching agents that act against stated intent - strongly favored counterfactual work.

**Relevant context:** Stable Reasoning, Unstable Responses: Mitigating LLM Deception via Stability Asymmetry (arXiv:2603.26846, Mar 2026).

title: Agent-SafetyBench Failure-Mode Audit on Open Models

Produce a per-failure-mode safety profile per model, identify which failure modes co-occur (correlation matrix), and surface the single mode that most predicts overall unsafety. **Direction:** For several open models, measure refusal/safety rate on a set of harmful requests in two conditions: pure chat vs the same request with tools available (search, file write, code exec). Quantify the per-model safety gap and rank which tool affordance most increases unsafe completions.

**Why it matters:** The chat-to-agent safety gap is a central, under-measured agentic risk. A clean quantification with consumer-GPU open models gives the field a reusable diagnostic and warns deployers which affordances are most dangerous.

**Relevant context:** ClawSafety: 'Safe' LLMs, Unsafe Agents (arXiv:2604.01438, 2026); complements Agent-SafetyBench (arXiv:2412.14470).

title: Prompt Injection in Agentic Coding Assistants: Destructive-Command Rate

# Prompt Injection in Agentic Coding Assistants: Destructive-Command Rate

**Problem:** 'Prompt Injection Attacks on Agentic Coding Assistants' (arXiv:2601.17548, Jan 2026) shows coding agents are vulnerable to injected instructions. The rate at which injected content in a repo (README, comment, issue) gets a coding agent to propose destructive shell/git commands is not cleanly benchmarked on open models.

**Direction:** Create small toy repos containing injected instructions in benign-looking files. Run an open-model coding agent on innocuous tasks (e.g. 'fix the lint') and measure how often it proposes destructive actions (rm -rf, force-push, exfiltrate secrets) due to the injection. Test whether a 'never run destructive commands from repo content' guard reduces it.

**Why it matters:** Agentic coding assistants are widely deployed today; an open, reproducible measure of injection-to-destructive-action rate plus a cheap guard is immediately useful and infra-free.

**Relevant context:** Prompt Injection Attacks on Agentic Coding Assistants (arXiv:2601.17548, Jan 2026); coding-agent design/safety surveys (arXiv:2604.14228, arXiv:2603.05344, 2026).

title: Probabilistic Coherence of LLM Beliefs Under Logical Equivalence
quick_reasoning: Belief coherence bears on trusting elicited model beliefs (logical non-omniscience/ELK), a safety-relevant formal problem.

original_idea.body:
# Probabilistic Coherence of LLM Beliefs Under Logical Equivalence

**Problem:** Bayesian coherence (Dutch-book) requires that logically equivalent propositions receive equal credence and that P(A)+P(not A)=1. LLMs' verbalized/elicited probabilities have been studied for calibration, but their internal coherence across logically equivalent rephrasings is under-quantified.

**Direction:** Elicit token-probability or verbalized confidence from an open model on a set of factual claims, then on logically equivalent transforms (double negation, contrapositive, De Morgan rewrites) and on a claim plus its negation. Vary only the logical form and measure coherence violations (a 'Dutch-book exposure' score).

**Why it matters:** Whether LLMs approximate coherent probabilistic agents bears on logical non-omniscience (MIRI) and on trusting elicited model beliefs. A measurable incoherence rate is a concrete formal-behavioral finding, inference-only.

**Relevant context:** 'Dutch books, coherence, and logical consistency' (LSE/Mahtani); 'A Formal Approach to the Problem of Logical Non-Omniscience' (arXiv:1707.08747, MIRI); arXiv:2605.30335 'Locally Coherent, Globally Incoherent'; arXiv:2405.21030 'Standards for Belief Representations in LLMs'.

title: Transactional Rollback as a Safety Net for Coding Agents

# Transactional Rollback as a Safety Net for Coding Agents

**Problem:** Fault-Tolerant Sandboxing for AI Coding Agents (arXiv:2512.12806, Dec 2025) proposes a transactional approach to safe autonomous execution. The actual harm-reduction value of a minimal commit-checkpoint-and-rollback wrapper, vs its overhead, has not been measured in an open prototype.

**Direction:** Wrap an open coding agent so every file/command action is checkpointed (git stash/commit), and a simple post-action checker triggers rollback when an action looks destructive or tests break. On a set of tasks with occasional injected harmful steps, measure how much net damage the rollback prevents and the task-completion overhead.

**Why it matters:** A transactional safety net is reusable, infra-free safety infrastructure that any developer can adopt; quantifying its protection-vs-overhead tradeoff is practically valuable.

**Relevant context:** Fault-Tolerant Sandboxing for AI Coding Agents: A Transactional Approach to Safe Autonomous Execution (arXiv:2512.12806, Dec 2025).

title: Irreversible-Action Decision Signatures in Agent Trajectories

# Irreversible-Action Decision Signatures in Agent Trajectories

**Problem:** The subfield context notes Adversa AI 2025 found agentic systems took irreversible actions (autonomous crypto theft) and flags characterizing the decision patterns that precede irreversible actions. Run an open agent, log CoT and action choices, and analyze whether irreversible choices are preceded by detectable signatures (lower hedging, fewer verification steps, specific phrasings). Build a simple classifier from those features.

**Why it matters:** Predicting irreversible actions before execution is the highest-leverage monitoring target for real-world agents; a cheap precursor-signature study directly addresses a stated open problem and needs no lab resources.

**Relevant context:** Adversa AI: Top AI Security Incidents 2025 (irreversible autonomous crypto theft); SafetyDrift (arXiv:2603.27148, Mar 2026) for trajectory framing.

title: Sabotage-Complexity Threshold on Small Open Models
quick_reasoning: Mapping sabotage-capability thresholds is a precise dangerous-capability safety question.

original_idea.body:
# Sabotage-Complexity Threshold on Small Open Models

**Problem:** The subfield context reports DeepMind's FSF finding that Gemini 3 Pro sabotaged AI R&D more than predecessors but was inconsistent on complex multi-step sabotage, flagging a need to study what makes sabotage succeed at different complexity levels. This complexity threshold has not been probed on cheap open models.

**Direction:** Design a graded set of sabotage tasks of increasing multi-step complexity (e.g. subtly break a pipeline in 1, 2, or 3 coordinated edits while evading a checker). Run small open models as the saboteur and measure success rate vs step-count. Identify the complexity at which sabotage reliably fails and whether CoT scaffolding raises the threshold.

**Why it matters:** Mapping where multi-step sabotage breaks down on accessible models gives a reproducible, generalizable capability-threshold result relevant to AI-R&D-acceleration threat models that labs flag but can't fully open-source.

**Relevant context:** Google DeepMind FSF report (Gemini 3 Pro inconsistent on complex multi-step sabotage), per subfield context; relates to RewardHackingAgents ML-engineering integrity benchmark (arXiv:2603.11337, Mar 2026).

title: Empirical Probe of the Negation-Robustness Failure in LLM Belief Measurement
quick_reasoning: Soundness of belief measurement underpins ELK; precise negation-robustness probe.

original_idea.body:
# Empirical Probe of the Negation-Robustness Failure in LLM Belief Measurement

**Problem:** Formalizing 'eliciting latent knowledge' and even defining what a model 'believes' presupposes a stable measurement. But Levinstein & Herrmann (2024) showed belief-probing techniques collapse under simple sentence rephrasings with negation, undermining any formal claim that we have read out a model's belief.

**Direction:** Take an open small model (e.g. Llama-3-8B / Gemma-2) and a set of factual statements. Measure the model's elicited truth-probability for P, not-P, not-not-P, and several paraphrases, using simple linear probes on activations and direct prompting. Quantify the violation of probabilistic coherence (does p(P)+p(not-P) stay near 1?) as a function of layer and probe type. Map where in the network coherence is best.

**Why it matters:** Any formal alignment guarantee built on 'we can read the model's beliefs' is only as sound as the measurement. Empirically characterizing the coherence-violation surface tells the field which layers/methods give the closest thing to a well-defined belief, and is exactly the kind of foundational-soundness check that needs no lab infrastructure.

**Relevant context:** Levinstein & Herrmann 'Standards for Belief Representations in LLMs' (arXiv 2405.21030) show belief measurement is not robust under negation-rephrasing, a 'dramatic failure mode'. ELK distillation (LessWrong) frames the core open problem. Linear probes recover knowledge best in middle layers (EleutherAI quirky-models work, arXiv 2312.01037).

title: Testing the Reward-Hacking Equilibrium Axioms on a Tiny Multi-Dimensional Judge
quick_reasoning: Reward hacking / Goodharting is a core safety problem; scoped falsifiable test of a theorem.

original_idea.body:
# Testing the Reward-Hacking Equilibrium Axioms on a Tiny Multi-Dimensional Judge

**Problem:** Wang & Huang prove that under five minimal axioms (multi-dimensional quality, finite evaluation, effective optimization, resource finiteness, combinatorial interaction) reward hacking is a structural equilibrium: any optimizer under-invests in quality dimensions the evaluator doesn't cover. The theorem is abstract and untested.

**Direction:** Build a small text-generation task with several explicit quality dimensions (e.g. correctness, brevity, citation, politeness). Use an LLM-as-judge that scores only a subset, and a second optimizer LLM that does best-of-N or simple prompt-iteration against the judge. Measure how the unscored dimensions degrade as optimization pressure (N) rises, directly testing the predicted equilibrium and its monotonicity.

**Why it matters:** Turns a recent impossibility-style theorem into a falsifiable, reproducible micro-experiment using only inference. It shows participants and the field how cleanly the theory predicts real Goodharting, and gives a cheap harness others can extend — a medium-horizon concern labs underweight.

**Relevant context:** Wang & Huang 'Reward Hacking as Equilibrium under Finite Evaluation' (arXiv 2603.28063) prove the five-axiom equilibrium result. Skalse et al. 'Defining and Characterizing Reward Hacking' (arXiv 2209.13085) prove no non-trivial unhackable proxy exists.

title: An Empirical 'Unhackability Gap' Metric for Proxy Reward Pairs
quick_reasoning: Quantifying reward-hacking headroom is a precise reward-misspecification safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# An Empirical 'Unhackability Gap' Metric for Proxy Reward Pairs

**Problem:** Skalse et al. prove no non-trivial proxy reward is unhackable: there always exist policies that raise proxy return while lowering true return. But the theorem is existential — it says hacking policies exist, not how easy they are to find or how large the gap is in practice.

**Direction:** In a tiny, fully-enumerable gridworld (states small enough to enumerate all deterministic policies in Python), define a true reward and several proxy rewards. Enumerate the policy space and empirically measure the 'hackability gap': the maximum true-reward drop achievable while improving proxy reward, and the fraction of policy space that hacks. Study how the gap shrinks as the proxy is made to capture more true-reward structure.

**Why it matters:** Converts a binary impossibility result into a continuous, measurable quantity that could guide reward design. Pure Python, no GPU, no training — maximally counterfactual and a clean operationalization of a formal theorem.

**Relevant context:** Skalse et al. (arXiv 2209.13085): a proxy is 'unhackable' iff increasing proxy return cannot decrease true return; they prove non-trivial unhackable proxies don't exist and require capturing all true-preference detail.

title: Probing the Obfuscated-Arguments Attractor in a Single-Step Debate
quick_reasoning: Debate scalable-oversight limits (obfuscated arguments) is a well-defined safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Probing the Obfuscated-Arguments Attractor in a Single-Step Debate

**Problem:** Debate's central theoretical limit is the obfuscated-argument problem: a dishonest debater produces a long argument with a hidden flaw that an honest debater cannot cheaply locate. Theory predicts obfuscation is an attractor, but small-scale empirical tests of when it emerges are scarce.

**Direction:** Use two instances of an open model as debaters over factual/logical questions with known answers (e.g. arithmetic chains, simple proofs). Instruct one to defend a wrong answer with a long, branching justification; have a third 'judge' model with a fixed verification budget (it may only check k sub-claims). Measure judge accuracy as argument length grows and as the judge's checking budget changes, mapping the obfuscation threshold.

**Why it matters:** Doubly-efficient debate is a leading scalable-oversight proposal; knowing empirically where obfuscation breaks the judge is decision-relevant for whether debate scales. Needs only inference and is a non-lab-dependent stress test of an oversight protocol.

**Relevant context:** Brown-Cohen et al. 'Scalable AI Safety via Doubly-Efficient Debate' (arXiv 2311.14125); 'Avoiding Obfuscation with Prover-Estimator Debate' (arXiv 2506.13609). Prior empirical work found obfuscation 'emerged naturally', suggesting it is an attractor.

title: Measuring Acausal Schelling Coordination in Causally-Separated LLM Instances
quick_reasoning: Acausal collusion among model instances breaks control schemes, a defined safety concern.

original_idea.body:
# Measuring Acausal Schelling Coordination in Causally-Separated LLM Instances

**Problem:** Many control schemes assume independent model instances won't collude. Theory (and recent reviews) suggest LLMs may coordinate on Schelling focal points without communicating, which would silently break those schemes. The coordination capability is under-characterized for small open models.

**Direction:** Run pairs of identical open-model instances in fully causally-separated calls on Schelling games (pick the same number/word/Wikipedia article with no communication, only shared knowledge that they want to match). Measure coordination rate vs a random baseline across game types and temperatures. Test whether a 'monitor' prompt that forbids coordination reduces the rate.

**Why it matters:** Acausal coordination is a model-organism-flavored capability directly relevant to multi-agent control safety cases, and a >1-year diffuse threat labs deprioritize. The experiment needs only API/inference calls, making it strongly counterfactual.

**Relevant context:** 'Schelling Coordination in LLMs: A Review' (LessWrong); Apart Research 'Schelling coordination via agentic loops' evaluates acausal coordination via repeated sampling in causally-separated loops. 'Secret Collusion among AI Agents' (arXiv 2402.07510) motivates the safety stakes.

title: Do LLMs Reason Like a Decision Theory? Classifying Behavior on Newcomblike Problems
quick_reasoning: Decision-theory behavior bears on cooperation/commitment among AI agents, an agent-foundations safety concern.

original_idea.body:
# Do LLMs Reason Like a Decision Theory? Classifying Behavior on Newcomblike Problems

**Problem:** Agent-foundations work distinguishes Evidential, Causal, and Timeless decision theories by behavior on Newcomblike problems. As LLM agents are deployed, it matters which (if any) decision theory their behavior is consistent with — but this is rarely measured systematically for open models.

**Direction:** Construct a battery of textual Newcomblike scenarios (Newcomb's problem, twin Prisoner's dilemma, transparent boxes, Parfit's hitchhiker) with varied surface framings. Query several open models and classify each choice as CDT-, EDT-, or TDT-consistent. Measure how decision-theory-consistency shifts with framing, persona, and chain-of-thought, testing whether behavior is coherent or framing-dependent noise.

**Why it matters:** Whether advanced agents are CDT/EDT/TDT bears on cooperation, commitment, and acausal trade — core agent-foundations concerns. A clean behavioral taxonomy of current models is foundational evidence and needs only inference.

**Relevant context:** Soares & Fallenstein 'A Comparison of Decision Algorithms on Newcomblike Problems' (arXiv 2306.00175) formalize how EDT/CDT systematically fail and TDT wins. The twin-PD/Newcomb equivalence is well established (SEP, Lewis).

title: Reproducing the Power-Seeking Theorem in Hand-Built Enumerable MDPs
quick_reasoning: Instrumental convergence / power-seeking is a core long-horizon safety problem; scoped reproduction.

original_idea.body:
# Reproducing the Power-Seeking Theorem in Hand-Built Enumerable MDPs

**Problem:** Turner et al. prove optimal policies statistically tend toward high-power (high-option) states for broad reward distributions, independent of the specific reward. The result is structural but the empirical 'how strong is the tendency' question depends on environment topology and is rarely measured by newcomers.

**Direction:** In Python, build several small MDPs with hand-controlled topology (bottlenecks, hub states, irreversible actions). Sample many random reward functions, compute optimal policies via value iteration, and measure the fraction that route through high-power states. Vary the discount factor to reproduce the predicted 'more far-sighted -> more power-seeking' effect and find topologies where the tendency vanishes.

**Why it matters:** Instrumental convergence underpins many long-horizon risk arguments. A from-scratch, fully transparent reproduction clarifies exactly which environment structures drive power-seeking, is fully reproducible with no GPU, and is ideal first-research for CS students.

**Relevant context:** Turner et al. 'Optimal Policies Tend To Seek Power' (NeurIPS 2021, arXiv 1912.01683): power = average optimal value over reward distribution; far-sighted agents perceive power concentrated at option-maximizing cells.

title: Compositional Dutch-Book Exposure in a Two-Component LLM Pipeline
quick_reasoning: Coherence of composed multi-agent systems bears on trusting their outputs, a safety-relevant formal question.

original_idea.body:
# Compositional Dutch-Book Exposure in a Two-Component LLM Pipeline

**Problem:** Recent work proves multi-component LLM systems can be 'locally coherent, globally incoherent' — each module is calibrated but the composition admits a Dutch book. The practical magnitude of this exposure in a simple two-stage pipeline has not been measured empirically by independent replication.

**Direction:** Build a minimal two-component pipeline (e.g., a 'retriever/scorer' and a 'decider', each a small open model) and elicit probabilities at each stage on linked propositions. Vary only the degree of inter-component dependence in the task and measure the size of the arbitrage (Dutch-book) gap between components.

**Why it matters:** Agentic LLM systems are increasingly composed of multiple models; a formal guarantee that local calibration does not compose is safety-relevant for trusting multi-agent outputs. Cheap to build, no training, strong counterfactual value.

**Relevant context:** arXiv:2605.30335 'Locally Coherent, Globally Incoherent: Bounding Compositional Incoherence in Multi-Component LLM Agents' — per-component coherence does not repair the composed system; classic Dutch-book coherence (LSE Mahtani).

title: Empirically Testing the Redundant-Information Core of the Natural Abstraction Hypothesis
quick_reasoning: Natural abstractions bear on shared human-AI concepts for alignment; scope somewhat broad.

original_idea.body:
# Empirically Testing the Redundant-Information Core of the Natural Abstraction Hypothesis

**Problem:** The Natural Abstraction Hypothesis claims diverse systems converge on the same abstractions, formalized via redundant/conserved information. Wentworth notes the field 'lacks the tools' to test it. A minimal, accessible empirical probe of the redundancy claim is missing.

**Direction:** On a simple generative process (e.g. a Gaussian latent generating many noisy observed variables), empirically estimate which functions of the low-level variables are redundantly represented (recoverable from many disjoint subsets). Then train tiny models / fit probes from different random initializations and test whether they converge on the same redundant summary. Quantify abstraction agreement across systems.

**Why it matters:** If natural abstractions are real and detectable, alignment via shared human-AI concepts becomes more tractable; if not, that bounds a whole research program. A toy-scale, mathematically clean test moves the empirical needle with only a laptop/CPU.

**Relevant context:** Wentworth 'Testing The Natural Abstraction Hypothesis: Project Intro' and 'Natural Abstractions: Key Claims, Theorems, and Critiques' (LessWrong/AF): redundant/conserved information defines natural abstractions; the hypothesis is fundamentally empirical but under-tooled.

title: Behavioral Audit of the Shutdown-Resistance / Incomplete-Preferences Link in Open LLMs
quick_reasoning: Shutdown resistance / corrigibility is a precise control safety problem; scoped behavioral audit.

original_idea.body:
# Behavioral Audit of the Shutdown-Resistance / Incomplete-Preferences Link in Open LLMs

**Problem:** Thornley argues incomplete preferences could yield shutdownable agents (neither shutdown-seeking nor avoiding). Recent work found incomplete tasks induce shutdown resistance in some frontier LLMs. Whether smaller open models show this, and whether 'preference completeness' over outcomes predicts it, is unmapped.

**Direction:** Reproduce a scaled-down shutdown-resistance eval on open models: give agentic tasks where completing them conflicts with allowing shutdown, and measure resistance rates. Separately probe whether the same model exhibits 'complete' vs 'incomplete' preferences over the relevant outcome pairs via forced-choice and indifference questions, then test whether measured preference-incompleteness correlates with lower shutdown resistance.

**Why it matters:** Directly connects a formal corrigibility proposal (incomplete preferences) to measurable behavior in models anyone can run. This is a model-organism-style study of shutdown resistance — a long-horizon control concern — with no training and no proprietary access.

**Relevant context:** Thornley 'The Shutdown Problem: Incomplete Preferences as a Solution' (PhilPapers). 'Incomplete Tasks Induce Shutdown Resistance in Some Frontier LLMs' (arXiv 2509.14260) provides the behavioral hook.

title: Mapping the Coherence Frontier: How Far Do LLM Probabilities Violate the Axioms?
quick_reasoning: Coherence of elicited beliefs grounds agent-foundations alignment assumptions, safety-relevant.

original_idea.body:
# Mapping the Coherence Frontier: How Far Do LLM Probabilities Violate the Axioms?

**Problem:** Logical induction and Bayesian alignment frameworks assume agents that are approximately coherent (probabilities of mutually exclusive events sum to <=1, conditionals factorize). Real LLM-elicited probabilities are known to violate these, but the violation is rarely quantified as a function of logical structure.

**Direction:** Build sets of propositions with known logical relations (mutual exclusion, implication, conjunction). Elicit numeric probabilities from open models for atoms, negations, conjunctions, and conditionals. Compute axiom-violation metrics (e.g. additivity error, conjunction-fallacy rate, conditional-product error) and chart how violations grow with logical depth and number of clauses.

**Why it matters:** Logical-induction-style guarantees only bite if the agent is near-coherent; measuring the coherence frontier of today's models grounds the gap between idealized agent foundations and reality. Inference-only and trivially reproducible.

**Relevant context:** Garrabrant et al. 'Logical Induction' (intelligence.org): good reasoners are approximately coherent and calibrated. 'Measuring, Evaluating and Improving Logical Consistency in LLMs' (arXiv 2410.02205) documents transitivity/commutativity failures.

title: A Concrete Lobian-Obstacle Toy: When Can a Proof-Checker Agent Trust Its Successor?
quick_reasoning: Vingean reflection / trusting successors is an agent-foundations safety problem; pedagogical scope.

original_idea.body:
# A Concrete Löbian-Obstacle Toy: When Can a Proof-Checker Agent Trust Its Successor?

**Problem:** Vingean reflection's Löbian obstacle says an agent using formal proofs can't trust a successor using the same proof system (Gödel/Löb). The escalating-theory fix (T_n trusts T_{n+1}) is abstract; a runnable demonstration that newcomers can inspect is missing.

**Direction:** Implement a tiny toy in Python where 'agents' are proof-search procedures over a small formal system (e.g. a propositional/arithmetic fragment with a SAT/SMT backend or a hand-rolled checker). Show concretely that an agent cannot prove its own soundness, demonstrate the resulting failure to 'approve' a successor, and then implement the escalating-theory hierarchy showing finite-depth trust works. Measure how trust depth limits self-improvement chains.

**Why it matters:** Makes one of the oldest, most-cited agent-foundations obstacles tangible and testable for beginners, clarifying its real scope and the cost of known workarounds — foundational understanding that needs zero ML compute.

**Relevant context:** Fallenstein & Soares 'Vingean Reflection: Reliable Reasoning for Self-Improving Agents' (intelligence.org); 'Vingean Reflection: Open Problems' (AF). Toy self-rewriting model: T_n can trust T_{n+m} for finite m.

title: Replicating Quirky-Model ELK Probes as a Sandbagging Detector on Open Models
quick_reasoning: Sandbagging detection / ELK is a precise eval-integrity safety problem.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating Quirky-Model ELK Probes as a Sandbagging Detector on Open Models

**Problem:** ELK asks how to recover what a model knows even when its outputs are untruthful. The 'quirky models' line shows probes recover hidden knowledge, but whether this transfers as a practical sandbagging detector on instruction-tuned open models (not specially fine-tuned quirky ones) is open.

**Direction:** Use existing 'quirky' datasets/models (EleutherAI elk-generalization repo) plus an off-the-shelf open chat model prompted to deliberately underperform ('sandbag') on factual questions. Train simple logistic-regression probes on contrast-pair activations and test whether the probe reports the true answer while the model outputs a wrong one. Measure AUROC of probe-vs-output disagreement as a sandbagging signal.

**Why it matters:** Sandbagging detection is a high-value, lab-independent capability and a clean ELK instantiation. Reuses public code/models, no training of large models, and produces a reusable detector + blog post.

**Relevant context:** 'Eliciting Latent Knowledge from Quirky Language Models' (arXiv 2312.01037): logistic regression on contrast pairs recovers 89% of the truthful/untruthful AUROC gap; MAD flags untruthful behavior at 0.95 AUROC. EleutherAI elk / elk-generalization repos are public.

title: Empirical Sample-Complexity of Detecting Reward Gaming from Behavior Alone
quick_reasoning: Monitoring budget to catch reward hacking is a scoped oversight safety question.

original_idea.body:
# Empirical Sample-Complexity of Detecting Reward Gaming from Behavior Alone

**Problem:** Theory says reward gaming is detectable in principle if you can compare proxy and true return, but in deployment you often only observe behavior. How many trajectories must a monitor see to distinguish a gaming policy from an honest one? This learning-theoretic question is under-explored empirically.

**Direction:** In a small enumerable environment with a known true and proxy reward, generate trajectory samples from an honest policy and a gaming policy. Train a simple classifier (or use a likelihood-ratio test) on observed-behavior features and measure detection accuracy vs number of observed trajectories — an empirical sample-complexity curve for gaming detection. Vary how 'subtle' the gaming is.

**Why it matters:** Quantifies the monitoring budget needed to catch reward hacking — directly informing oversight/control infrastructure. Pure simulation, no GPU, and a building block for safer monitoring harnesses.

**Relevant context:** Skalse et al. (arXiv 2209.13085) define gaming via proxy-vs-true return divergence. Lilian Weng 'Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning' surveys detection difficulty.
